families.name: From a certificate to a profile
From cell data to the certificate

topics.name: The blow-up statements
topics.description: Smooth solutions, breakdown on space and on the torus, and the theorems that state them (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1).

topics.name: The fractional extension
topics.description: The authors' separate extension with dissipation exponent between 1 and 5/4, outside the classical paper.

topics.name: Heat flow and mild solutions
topics.description: The heat semigroup, the bilinear Duhamel term, mild solutions, restarting and uniqueness (§3).

topics.name: Recurrent profiles
topics.description: Self-similar time-periodic profiles, their slices and orbits, and weak profiles read as physical fields (§2, §4.1, §7.11).

topics.name: Monodromy and the correction
topics.description: The period map, its compact-plus-small splitting, the spectral projection and the fixed point that corrects a profile to an exact solution (§4).

topics.name: Passing to the torus
topics.description: The solenoidal cutoff, periodization and the periodic right inverse that move the construction onto the torus (§5–6).

topics.name: From certificate to profile
topics.description: Certificate data, the free operator, convection, held solutions and the smoothing of the weak profile they produce (§7).

topics.name: The coercive multiplier estimate
topics.description: The multiplier, its five density coefficients and lower bound, and the a priori estimate it gives (Appendix B.1 and B.2).

topics.name: Encoded cell data
topics.description: The finitely represented inputs: coordinates and harmonics, the profile representation, splines and jets, physical cells, rows, weights and potentials.

topics.name: Reduction to the quarter plane
topics.description: Symmetry reduction of the density to the meridian quarter plane (B.3).

topics.name: Cells, traces and tails
topics.description: Integrability, the common vector of unknowns, resolved modes, the tail budget and the exterior estimate (B.4).

topics.name: Angular and ray-exterior tests
topics.description: The angular inequalities, the pointwise test and the integrated test on ray exteriors (B.5 and B.6).

topics.name: The matrix tree lower bound
topics.description: The tree conditions on the cell matrices and the passage from all cells to the global inequality (B.7 and B.8).

topics.name: Changing the profile
topics.description: Bounds for moving estimates from the reference field to the actual profile (B.9).

topics.name: The adjoint pairing and its error
topics.description: The quadratic adjoint pairing, the azimuthal dual norm and the linear adjoint error with potentials and pins (B.10 to B.12).

topics.name: The offset and the certificate
topics.description: Enclosing the constant, linear and quadratic offset, and the fifteen fields of CellSystemCondition that make the data a certificate (B.13 and B.14).

notes.Breakdown.Freq.BilinSpec: The interaction is specified by all its Hilbert-space pairings. This permits the nonlinear term to be defined without taking a pointwise Fourier transform of each physical product.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.BilinExists.bili: The symmetric trilinear pairing is unchanged when its two velocity inputs are interchanged. Existence of the corresponding bounded bilinear operator and its physical heat-Leray formula are separate results.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.GradSixDecay.cut: The cutoff is smooth, equals one on the radius-R ball and vanishes outside the radius-2R ball when R > 0. Completion of the physical homogeneous Sobolev space requires the surrounding approximation argument.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.GradSixDecay.mem: Inverse-radius decay makes the sixth power integrable in three dimensions. Membership in the full homogeneous gradient space also requires gradient integrability and the embedding result.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.cutof: For each Schwartz potential and positive error tolerance, the theorem chooses one compact solenoidal approximation. Applying those choices along a sequence gives the approximation used in the exposition.
The cutoff curl is smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free. A separate convergence theorem controls both its gradient error and the gradient error of its negative Laplacian.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceApprox.symbo: The weighted curl identities hold almost everywhere, so the single frequency ξ = 0 does not affect them. The measure-zero observation is more general than this particular application.

The result constructs a Schwartz potential for each smooth annular symbol and identifies its curl at nonzero frequencies. Convergence of an approximating sequence also uses the preceding L² approximation estimates.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceDense.div_pr: The transverse projection has zero contraction with ξ, enforcing the solenoidal Fourier condition. Identifying its output with a physical divergence-free field uses the Fourier correspondence.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceDense.norm_p: The transverse projection is contractive at each frequency. Smoothness of projected symbols requires support away from zero, and the error estimate for reality averaging requires a target with the corresponding symmetry.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceDense.smooth: The smoothing result starts with an L² field already supported on a compact annulus. Truncating a general field to such annuli and passing to a convergent sequence are separate steps.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.NiceDense.symFie: A real physical field has Fourier symmetry m(−ξ) = conjugate(m(ξ)). Averaging a symbol with its reflected conjugate imposes this symmetry.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.Internal.VelocityExists.i: Closure under addition applies once both summands are known to be compact smooth solenoidal fields. The finite-dimensional section construction supplies that property for the selected correction.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.IsWeakSolution: The weak-solution class assumes smooth decaying slices and L²-continuous time differences, in addition to the solenoidal test equation and continuity in X. The general physical weak-to-mild statement has a wider input class.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.X: The Fourier variable represents one homogeneous derivative of velocity. The continuous map into L⁶ recovers the physical velocity and fixes its additive-constant ambiguity.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.bilinCompact_holds: Compactness is proved for coefficients in the dense span of compact solenoidal test fields. The bilinear bound and operator-norm closure extend it to every coefficient in X.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.bilinX: The interaction is defined by its pairings with a heat-smoothed test field. The projected physical nonlinearity is identified with this operator by separate Fourier and velocity identities.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.heatDivFree: The output represents one homogeneous derivative of the physical velocity. Its multiplier therefore includes 2π|ξ| alongside the heat factor and the Leray projection; the physical Oseen tensor needs a separate identification.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.longitudinal: This is the longitudinal projection ξ⊗ξ/|ξ|². Subtracting it from the identity gives the transverse Leray projection; the real Fourier space also imposes conjugation symmetry.
notes.Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds: The formal proof obtains the mild equation from density of Fourier test fields and their Laplacians. The paper uses the cited weak-to-mild theorem for the corresponding physical argument.
notes.Breakdown.HeatBilinear.HasCompactKernel: Only compactness on a dense set of coefficients is needed for the transfer argument. The Fourier proof uses frequency restriction, equicontinuity and tail control; the physical-space proof uses local compactness of Sobolev restriction.
notes.Breakdown.IsSimilarityProfile: The assumption includes decay of ∇²W and ∇q. Appendix A derives those estimates analytically from the paper’s profile assumptions; that derivation is not supplied by this definition.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.Cutoff.Internal.contD: The homotopy integrand is smooth in the integration parameter and spatial position for a fixed smooth field. The time-dependent application additionally tracks the smooth dependence of that field on time.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.Cutoff.Internal.hasFD: The differentiation theorem concerns the spatial parameter of an integral over [0,1]. Joint smoothness in physical time requires including that additional parameter in the argument.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.InverseAlgebra.Intern: If ‖Q‖ ≤ q < 1, the inverse of I − Q has norm at most (1 − q)⁻¹. The bound is valid on any Banach space used for the periodic inverse construction.
For an operator of norm below one, the inverse of I − Q satisfies z − Qz = y. This is the cancellation described by the convergent geometric series in the exposition.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellDefs.Internal.ad: The local transport estimate includes the factor |B|¹ᐟ³ when converting L⁶ data to L² on the support ball. The full radial-extension construction and weighted-path bound need further arguments.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.e: The result is the interpolation inequality ‖f‖₃ ≤ ‖f‖₂¹ᐟ²‖f‖₆¹ᐟ². The period-uniform Sobolev inequality used after it is a separate ingredient.
The scalar estimate controls (1 + y)e⁻ʸˢ for s > 0 and y ≥ 0. The separate bound involving r¹ᐟ²e⁻ʳ needs its own elementary estimate.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.s: The duality argument treats compactly supported L² forcing after scaling to the unit torus, using the periodic Sobolev estimate and μτ ≤ 1. Extension to arbitrary L³ᐟ² forcing and all periods needs the additional physical argument.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.ShellTorus.Internal.v: Every coordinate plane has zero three-dimensional volume. Consequently the unit-cell boundary is negligible for Fourier norm identities and for identifying the wrapping map with the identity.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.TorusBlowup: The intermediate conclusion gives a smooth periodic datum and an unbounded periodic mild trajectory. Two-sided rates and convergence to the physical profile are additional quantitative statements.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffGradientClose: The estimate keeps a fixed physical cutoff near the centre of the unit torus and lets the remaining time shrink. The large-radius formulation is obtained by expressing the same geometry in similarity coordinates.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.heatDivFreeComparison: The formal projected-heat comparison is uniform on a time window [ε,ε⁻¹]. Short times are estimated separately when assembling the inverse; the paper’s Oseen argument gives explicit bounds across the full positive-time range.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.homotopyCurl: The identity holds for every smooth divergence-free spatial field and every centre. In the profile construction it is applied to each time slice.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.movingFrameReduction: A periodic velocity permits pressure with a spatially affine part. The construction removes that part by a time-dependent velocity shift and translation chosen to preserve the initial datum.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.shellInverseTransfer: The theorem eliminates the free shift, solves a reduced equation on the restriction space, and reconstructs the periodic path. Its two comparison bounds and maximum product norm must also be verified when applying it to the continuous weighted spaces.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.transplantField: The compact field is placed about (1/2,1/2,1/2) in the unit cell. A spatial translation moves that centre to the origin used in the large-torus exposition.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.transplantNorm: The periodic norm is the full H¹ norm, so the identity includes μ‖f‖²₂ in addition to ‖∇f‖²₂. The mass contribution tends to zero with μ.
notes.Breakdown.SmoothFlow.smooth_physField_cu: The input trajectory has every Sobolev order and satisfies its Fourier integral equation. These hypotheses give smooth physical velocity and pressure, including at the initial time; the full continuation alternative needs additional estimates.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.exists_dichotomy: On the exceptional range, the statement gives a lower bound for forward powers and asserts surjectivity. Together these express the inverse-power decay used in the paper.
notes.Breakdown.TransferHolds: The retained conclusion is existence of arbitrarily close data in a prescribed dense space, with rescaled convergence to the orbit. The paper’s fixed finite-dimensional correction for every nearby datum is a further description of the construction.
notes.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.integ: The scalar integral equals 4c¹ᐟ⁴. In the general Duhamel theorem, the quantitative vector bound uses t − a ≤ 1, while integrability and continuity hold on arbitrary finite intervals.
notes.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.kern_: The assumed singular estimate is restricted to heat time at most one. On longer intervals the proof uses a bound of the form C_K(r⁻³ᐟ⁴ + 1), which still gives integrability.
notes.Breakdown.compactPiece_of: The argument extends endpoint compactness from dense simple coefficients by closedness of compact operators in operator norm. The exposition gives a sequential proof of that general closedness fact.
notes.Breakdown.contraction: The conclusion bounds the initial correction and returns a bounded interval sequence. Its proof chooses the correction from the first component of the right inverse, so membership in the exceptional range also requires that inverse’s range property.
notes.Breakdown.exists_section: The section lifts the exceptional component into the chosen dense data space. Its values may also have a stable component, which must remain in the forward evolution.
notes.Breakdown.monodromy: The formal proof subdivides a similarity period until each interval linearisation has norm at most one quarter. Identifying its endpoint product with the paper’s full-period Volterra map uses uniqueness of the linearised equation.
notes.Breakdown.orbitNorm: A slice below the small-data threshold generates a bounded solution through time one. Uniqueness and recurrence would then force the entire profile to vanish, giving the positive lower norm bound.
notes.Breakdown.orbitSeq: Each update is divided by the chosen decay factor. To obtain this recurrence from continuous forcing, first subtract the forcing path at the interval endpoints and then normalise.
notes.Breakdown.periodicInverse: The input is a bounded sequence of continuous paths on short intervals. Proposition 5.3 reconstructs the corresponding continuous weighted right inverse from this discrete mechanism.
notes.Breakdown.varConstIntegral: Integrability and continuity hold on every finite interval. The pure-power norm estimate requires t − a ≤ 1; the continuity proof uses a fixed integration domain and dominated convergence.
